title: IAG's Group-Wide SkyBreathe Rollout Is the Biggest Signal Yet That Fuel Efficiency Software Is Becoming Airline Infrastructure
summary: IAG's deployment of OpenAirlines' SkyBreathe across all five of its airlines and 600-plus aircraft is more than a procurement win — it's a signal about how airline groups are starting to treat fuel efficiency platforms as shared operational infrastructure rather than per-carrier point solutions.
body_markdown:
There's a meaningful difference between an airline buying fuel efficiency software and an airline group standardizing on a single fuel efficiency platform across all of its carriers. When IAG announced on September 29 that it had selected OpenAirlines' SkyBreathe for deployment across Aer Lingus, British Airways, Iberia, LEVEL, and Vueling, that distinction matters more than the headline number.

## A Portfolio Deal, Not a Point-Solution Purchase

<cite index="19-1">IAG has selected OpenAirlines' SkyBreathe fuel-efficiency platform for use across its five airlines, covering more than 600 aircraft.</cite> That scale alone is notable, but the more commercially significant detail is the architecture behind the deployment. <cite index="19-6">The rollout introduces a common data and reporting framework across the group, allowing IAG's airlines to measure fuel-efficiency performance more consistently and share initiatives.</cite> That's a different procurement logic than buying a tool to reduce fuel burn at one carrier — it's treating the software layer as group-wide operational infrastructure, the same way a large airline group might standardize on a single crew management or flight planning system.

<cite index="19-8">SkyBreathe is already in use at Aer Lingus, Iberia, LEVEL, and Vueling, with British Airways expected to complete its rollout in the coming months.</cite> That sequencing suggests the deal formalized a consolidation of deployments that were already happening organically across the group — which is actually a stronger commercial story than a clean greenfield win, because it implies OpenAirlines earned expansion across the portfolio one airline at a time before landing the group-level commitment.

## What the Cockpit-Facing Layer Actually Does

<cite index="19-4">SkyBreathe analyses data including flight plans, weather conditions, and aircraft performance to identify potential fuel-saving opportunities while maintaining safety standards.</cite> The analytical engine sits in the background, but SkyBreathe's pilot-facing module — MyFuelCoach — is where the flight deck angle comes in. <cite index="24-8,24-9">MyFuelCoach is an application pilots use during briefing and debriefing phases to see their individual performance, with precise recommendations based on their journey to help them make more informed decisions and improve environmental performance.</cite> That closes the loop between fleet-level data analysis and the individual crew member who can actually act on a recommendation in the cockpit. Without that layer, you have a reporting tool; with it, you have something that can actually change behavior at the point of flight.

Having spent time on the product and delivery side of flight ops software, I'd note that the hardest part of a deployment at this scale isn't the data integration — it's getting crews to engage with the feedback loop consistently enough that the platform generates real savings rather than just reports. <cite index="23-5,23-6">SkyBreathe is used by more than 80 airlines worldwide, and the platform harnesses advanced algorithms, artificial intelligence, and big data analytics to identify fuel-saving opportunities, delivering actionable recommendations to both operational teams and flight crews.</cite> That installed base gives OpenAirlines something genuinely valuable to offer a group like IAG: benchmarking data from a global operator community that no single-airline deployment can replicate.

## What This Means Competitively

For OpenAirlines, landing an IAG-scale group commitment is the kind of reference customer that changes conversations with every other airline group in Europe. <cite index="19-3">The platform is being deployed at Aer Lingus, British Airways, Iberia, LEVEL, and Vueling as airlines face continued pressure from volatile fuel prices.</cite> That volatility context matters commercially: when fuel costs are unpredictable, the business case for a platform that promises measurable reduction becomes easier to close across a finance committee — and IAG's CFO said as much in the announcement.

For the broader market, the interesting question is whether this represents the beginning of a consolidation pattern among European airline groups. Lufthansa Group, Air France-KLM, and others face the same multi-carrier, multi-AOC complexity that makes group-standardization appealing. Whether OpenAirlines can replicate the IAG playbook — organic adoption at the subsidiary level, followed by a group-level framework deal — is probably the most important strategic question for the company heading into 2027.

email_brief: On September 29, IAG announced a group-wide deployment of OpenAirlines' SkyBreathe fuel efficiency platform across all five of its airlines — Aer Lingus, British Airways, Iberia, LEVEL, and Vueling — covering more than 600 aircraft. The deal is notable because it isn't a fresh single-carrier win: SkyBreathe was already live at four of the five carriers, and the announcement formalized a group-level common data and reporting framework, essentially elevating the platform to shared operational infrastructure. This comes after OpenAirlines also signed Loganair in June 2026, making it a strong year of European expansion for the Toulouse-based startup. The strategic angle for today's post is what this pattern — organic subsidiary adoption followed by a group-level commitment — means for OpenAirlines' competitive position, and whether other European airline groups like Lufthansa or Air France-KLM are likely to follow a similar path.
